  "title": "Advantage-Decomposed Transition Scoring for Demonstration Curation via Dense Reward Models",
  "core_problem": "Existing demonstration curation methods operate in a single quality dimension — trajectory-level influence (CUPID, DataMIL, QoQ), scalar mutual information (DemInf), binary progress (GR-RL), or kinematic smoothness (RINSE) — and cannot distinguish whether a poor transition stems from being in a fundamentally bad state versus taking a bad action at an otherwise good state. Training-time advantage-weighted methods (AWR, AWAC, MARWIL, VACO) implicitly perform soft curation by reweighting gradient updates with exponentiated advantage, but (a) they couple the curation criterion to the training objective, so any downstream learner (VLA, Diffusion Policy, ACT) must re-derive the weighting, (b) they produce a single scalar weight per transition without separating state quality from action quality, and (c) they do not produce a reusable curated dataset. This conflation is consequential for imitation learning specifically: in demonstrations collected by heterogeneous operators, transitions at irrecoverable states (low V) where the operator's action happens to be locally 'best-possible' (moderate-to-high A) will receive high weight under A-only scoring but are harmful training signal — they teach behavior at states the policy should never reach. Conversely, mediocre actions at high-value states (high V, moderate A) may receive similar A-only weight to genuinely good transitions, diluting the signal. No current pre-training curation method makes the V×A distinction, because all collapse transition quality into a single scalar.",
  "opportunity": "Three developments converge to make two-dimensional, advantage-based pre-training curation both feasible and timely: (1) Pretrained dense reward models (Robometer, RSS 2026; RoboReward, Jan 2026) now provide frame-level reward signals validated across diverse embodiments, eliminating the sparse-reward degeneracy that would make naive IQL-based value decomposition encode only temporal position. Robometer's LIBERO-specific checkpoint provides calibrated rewards on the primary evaluation benchmark. (2) The theoretical machinery for causal advantage decomposition exists ('Skill or Luck?', ICLR 2024) but has never been applied to demonstration curation — it establishes that advantage captures the causal effect of the action on returns, which is precisely the decomposition needed for state-vs-action quality separation. (3) Training-time advantage-weighting methods (AWR, AWAC, MARWIL, VACO) have validated that advantage is a powerful curation signal, but remain coupled to specific training objectives and do not produce reusable curated datasets. The gap between training-time advantage weighting and pre-training 2D V×A dataset curation is the precise differentiator — and dense reward models make it realizable without requiring online interaction.",

QoQ (arXiv Mar 2026) uses per-sample influence with maximum-influence aggregation. (A2) Policy-driven selection: DataMIL (May 2025) trains datamodels to predict policy-level data influence across 60+ tasks including Open X-Embodiment. (A3) Statistical methods: DemInf (RSS 2025) scores trajectories by contribution to state-action mutual information via k-NN on VAE embeddings. (A4) Self-supervised methods: SCIZOR (ICRA 2026) uses temporal distance for progress prediction. Demo-SCORE (RSS 2025) trains success/failure classifiers from online rollouts. (A5) Smoothness heuristics: RINSE (ICML 2025) uses kinematic smoothness metrics (SAL, TED). (A6) Per-transition reweighting: PTR (Mar 2026) uses posterior-transition scoring via consequence encoding — reward-free and per-transition, but single-scalar weight. (B) Training-time advantage/value weighting (related but not directly competing — these modify optimization, not datasets): (B1) AWR (Peng et al. 2019) and MARWIL (Wang et al. 2018) weight BC updates by exponentiated advantage exp(A/τ). AWAC (Nair et al. 2020) extends AWR to offline-to-online settings. AW-Opt (Lu et al. 2022) scales advantage-weighted learning to real robots. (B2) VACO (ICLR 2025) uses a meta-scoring network driven by value estimation to weight each BC training sample via bi-level optimization — the most closely related training-time method. (B3) IDRL (ICLR 2025) iteratively removes zero-weight suboptimal transitions using learned visitation distribution ratios. (B4) ARFM (AAAI 2026) adaptively scales advantage signals in VLA flow matching loss; ReinboT (ICML 2025) predicts dense returns during VLA training. (C) Value-based assessment (complementary): GR-RL (Dec 2025) uses Q-values from sparse-reward offline RL as binary progress filters. 'Expert or not?' (ICLR 2026) uses Bellman-Wasserstein Distance for dataset-level quality assessment. V-GPS (CoRL 2024) uses offline RL value functions to re-rank action proposals at deployment time. (D) Reward models (infrastructure, not competing): Robometer (RSS 2026) provides dense frame-level rewards from a pretrained VLM trained on RBM-1M (1M+ trajectories), with validated LIBERO checkpoint. RoboReward (Jan 2026) provides alternative VLM-based dense rewards with RoboMimic-informed design. Key gap: All pre-training curation methods (A) produce single-scalar scores. All training-time methods (B) couple advantage weighting to specific training objectives. No method produces a reusable, 2D V×A-curated dataset that any downstream learner can consume.",
  "approach": "We propose Advantage-Decomposed Transition Scoring (ADTS), a pre-training curation pipeline that separates state quality from action quality to produce a reusable curated dataset consumable by any downstream policy learner. Stage 1 — Dense Reward Annotation: Apply the pretrained Robometer-LIBERO checkpoint to annotate every transition with dense frame-level reward. This replaces sparse binary rewards and is critical: dense rewards ensure the downstream value decomposition captures task-relevant quality rather than mere temporal position. Stage 2 — Advantage Decomposition: Train IQL (Kostrikov et al. 2022) on the dense-reward-annotated data to jointly learn Q(s,a) and V(s) via expectile regression. Compute per-transition advantage A(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s). This yields a two-dimensional V×A scoring space. Stage 3 — Quadrant-Aware Curation: Apply a smooth bivariate weighting function w(V,A) that implements quadrant-aware filtering: (i) high-V/high-A: fully weighted — good states with good actions; (ii) high-V/low-A: downweighted — operator errors at recoverable states, where the state shows this is a reachable good configuration but the action is suboptimal; (iii) low-V/high-A: conditionally preserved via a tunable temperature — these are potential hard examples (best-effort actions in difficult states) but also potential traps (locally 'optimal' actions in irrecoverable states); (iv) low-V/low-A: pruned — poor states with poor actions. Key differentiation from A-only weighting (AWR-style exp(A/τ)): A-only weighting cannot distinguish quadrant (iii) from quadrant (i), because both have high A. But for imitation learning, transitions in irrecoverable states (V≈0) with moderate A are harmful — they teach behavior at states the policy should never reach. Concrete constructed example: consider a tabletop manipulation task where the robot has knocked the object off the table. The state is irrecoverable (V≈0), but the robot's subsequent 'reaching' action may score moderate-to-high A because all actions at that state yield similar low returns (making the chosen action appear relatively optimal). A-only weighting preserves these transitions; V×A curation correctly identifies them as low-V and can prune or downweight them. We will verify this type of scenario exists empirically in LIBERO demonstrations with injected noise. Semantic Validation Protocol (mandatory before downstream training): (a) Verify V(s) correlates with human-annotated state quality (Spearman ρ > 0.6) on 50 annotated transitions per task; (b) Verify A(s,a) correlates with action quality annotations; (c) Measure V-A Pearson correlation; (d) If |r| > 0.5 (degeneracy), report this transparently and evaluate whether the V dimension still contributes via ablation. Fallback: if V and A are highly correlated across all tasks, ADTS gracefully degrades to approximately 1D scoring, and the contribution becomes the diagnostic framework for detecting when 2D curation adds value. Theoretical Contribution: We prove that under a dense reward model with bounded approximation error ε, there exist demonstration distributions (specifically, distributions with mixed failure modes combining irrecoverable-state transitions and operator-error transitions) where A-only curation via any monotone f(A) threshold provably selects a suboptimal training subset, while V×A quadrant-aware curation preserves the optimal subset. This is NOT the trivial claim that '2D contains more information than 1D' — it identifies the specific distributional structure (mixed failure modes with asymmetric V-A relationships) under which the V dimension is decision-relevant. Downstream Evaluation: Fine-tune OpenVLA-OFT (the current LIBERO SOTA at 97.1%) via LoRA on LIBERO (4 suites: Spatial, Object, Goal, Long) using ADTS-curated data at multiple curation ratios (100%, 75%, 50%, 33%). Compare against: (1) CUPID, (2) DemInf, (3) PTR, (4) RINSE, (5) A-only weighting baseline (exp(A/τ) using our dense-reward IQL, directly testing V's contribution), and (6) random subsampling. Additionally, compare conceptually against VACO by including VACO as a training-time baseline to show that pre-training curation achieves comparable or better results while being policy-agnostic. Ablations: (a) V-only vs A-only vs V×A curation; (b) dense reward (Robometer) vs sparse reward IQL; (c) weighting function temperature sensitivity; (d) empirical V-A correlation analysis across LIBERO suites.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 3)
Issues: ["LIBERO SATURATION: PLD (ICLR 2026, same conference cycle) achieves ~99% on LIBERO using residual RL + data generation, making OpenVLA-OFT's 97.1% no longer the undisputed SOTA. The ceiling for curation-based improvements on LIBERO is extremely small (~2.9% maximum headroom). The paper needs to reframe around data efficiency (same/better performance with 33-50% data) rather than absolute performance gains, or show complementarity with RL post-training.", "MISSING CRITICAL BASELINE — Robometer-reward-only curation: Robometer already demonstrates 'data retrieval for IL' as an application. The most natural baseline is using per-frame Robometer rewards directly as a curation signal (rank transitions by reward, prune low-reward ones) WITHOUT the IQL step. If this simple baseline performs comparably to ADTS's full V×A pipeline, the entire IQL decomposition is unnecessary overhead. This baseline is essential for justifying the method's complexity.", "NARROW EVALUATION SCOPE: LIBERO-only evaluation is a limitation for CoRL, where competing methods demonstrate broader applicability (DataMIL: 60+ tasks including Open X-Embodiment; CUPID: RoboMimic + real hardware). A single-benchmark paper needs exceptionally strong results and analysis to be accepted. Consider adding at least one additional benchmark (RoboMimic where Robometer's general checkpoint could be used).", "V/A DECOMPOSITION vs REWARD SIGNAL REDUNDANCY: With dense Robometer rewards, V(s) will essentially learn a smoothed cumulative reward (progress), and A(s,a) will capture deviations from expected progress. This may be highly correlated with simply using Robometer's per-frame reward and its temporal derivative. The paper must empirically demonstrate that IQL's V/A decomposition captures genuinely different information than what the raw reward signal already provides.", "THEORETICAL CONTRIBUTION NEEDS STRENGTHENING: The current theoretical result (A-only curation is suboptimal under mixed failure modes) is valid but modest — it identifies conditions under which 2D > 1D, which is somewhat expected. To strengthen: (a) provide sample complexity bounds showing V×A curation requires fewer demonstrations to achieve target performance, or (b) prove tighter characterization of when the V dimension is decision-relevant in terms of demonstration distribution statistics (e.g., mixture weights, state coverage overlap between failure modes)."]
Feedback: The idea has improved substantially across three rounds — the dense reward integration, semantic validation protocol, and AWR/VACO differentiation are all well-handled. Three specific changes would bring this to pass quality:

1. **Add Robometer-reward-only baseline and reframe contribution**: Include a baseline that uses Robometer's per-frame rewards directly for curation (e.g., prune transitions with reward below threshold, or weight by reward). This is the most dangerous ablation for the paper — if it works well, the IQL pipeline is unnecessary. But if ADTS significantly outperforms it, this becomes the paper's strongest evidence. Either way, intellectual honesty requires this comparison. Reframe around data efficiency rather than absolute LIBERO performance given PLD's 99%.

2. **Address LIBERO saturation explicitly**: Acknowledge PLD's ~99% result and frame ADTS as (a) complementary to RL post-training (curated data → better initialization → even RL benefits), (b) policy-agnostic (works with any downstream learner, not just the specific VLA used in PLD), and (c) focused on data efficiency (achieving comparable performance with less data). Show experiments at aggressive curation ratios (33%, 25%) where the value of intelligent curation is clearest.

3. **Add a second evaluation domain**: If timeline permits, add RoboMimic using Robometer's general checkpoint (not the LIBERO-specific one). Even 2-3 RoboMimic tasks would significantly strengthen the paper by demonstrating generalization beyond LIBERO. If not feasible for CoRL, at minimum acknowledge this limitation and present ICLR 2027 as the expanded evaluation target.

4. **Strengthen the ablation story**: The most compelling result would be: at 33% data retention, ADTS outperforms Robometer-reward-only curation, A-only weighting, random subsampling, AND the full-data baseline. This would simultaneously demonstrate that (a) curation matters, (b) 2D scoring matters, and (c) the V dimension specifically contributes. Structure the experiments around this narrative.

5. **Cite PLD and position carefully**: PLD (ICLR 2026) must be cited. Position ADTS as operating at a different level of the pipeline (data curation vs. policy optimization). Note that PLD's 99% is achieved with additional RL interaction + data generation, while ADTS works purely on existing demonstrations — different resource assumptions entirely.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求（每一轮修订都必须执行）

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化这个 idea 的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，建议用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
   - 搜索最新的相关论文（arXiv, conference proceedings）
   - 搜索 benchmark/leaderboard 确认当前 SOTA
   - 搜索可能遗漏的相关工作和 concurrent work

2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文的 abstract 和方法部分，
   不要只依赖搜索摘要。形成你自己对领域现状的独立判断。

3. **深度思考**：在修订之前，先独立思考以下问题：
   - 这个 idea 的核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach 来解决同一个核心问题？
   - 修订后的 idea 相比上一版有什么本质性的改进？

4. **避免表面修订**：如果你发现自己只是在换措辞或补充细节而没有实质改进，
   考虑是否需要 major revision 或 pivot。反复的 minor fix 不会拯救一个根基有问题的 idea。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，执行以下搜索流程：

1. **如果 reviewer 说'已有类似工作'**：
   - 搜索 reviewer 提到的论文，用 WebFetch 实际阅读
   - 搜索该论文的 cited-by，找到后续跟进工作
   - 明确你的 idea 与这些工作的差异化点——如果差异化不够，必须 pivot

2. **如果 reviewer 说'SOTA 过时'**：
   - 用 Papers With Code 查看当前排行榜
   - 搜索过去 6 个月的最新方法
   - 更新你的 landscape 和 baseline

3. **如果 reviewer 说'可行性有问题'**：
   - 搜索类似规模实验的实际成本和时间线
   - 搜索 GitHub 上是否有可复用的实现
   - 搜索相关数据集/模型的可获取性

4. **如果 reviewer 说'novelty 不足'**：
   - 对核心方法尽量做 3-5 种不同关键词组合的搜索
   - 搜索相邻领域是否有类似思路
   - 如果确实 novelty 不足，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- Use WebSearch to find updated information if the reviewer flagged outdated claims.
- You have full freedom in how much to change:
  - Minor fix: if only specific details are wrong, correct them and keep everything else.
  - Major revision: if the approach is fundamentally flawed but the core problem is valid, you may redesign the approach entirely.
  - Pivot: if the reviewer's feedback reveals that the core problem itself is invalid (e.g., the gap no longer exists), you may propose a RELATED but substantially different idea that builds on the same research area. This is preferred over forcing a doomed idea to pass review.
- The output replaces the original idea (same tracking ID). Whether you make a small tweak or a full pivot, output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields filled.
- In the output JSON, include a "change_type" field with one of: "minor", "major", or "pivot" to indicate the scope of your changes.
- Output the revised idea as a COMPLETE JSON object (same schema as original, plus "change_type").

## 停滞提醒
这个 idea 已经经过 3 轮修订，近 3 轮的平均分从 3.2 到 3.5，没有明显改善。

请认真思考：
- 当前方向是否存在根本性的瓶颈？反复的 minor fix 是否在回避核心问题？
- 如果你认为问题出在 approach 而非 framing，可以做 major revision。
- 如果你认为 core problem 本身就有问题（gap 不存在、问题不够重要），pivot 到同一研究领域下的新方向可能是更好的选择。
- 当然，如果你有信心这一轮修订能实现突破，继续改进也完全可以。

最终由你判断——做你认为最能提升 idea 质量的选择。

## PLD: Self-Improving Vision-Language-Action Models

PLD is a three-stage plug-and-play framework that improves VLAs through residual reinforcement learning (RL) and distribution-aware data collection.

**How it works:**

- In Stage 1 (specialist acquisition), the VLA backbone is frozen and lightweight residual actors are trained via off-policy RL, taking over in states where the base policy fails to probe failure regions.

- In Stage 2 (data collection), a hybrid rollout scheme biases residual interventions toward states frequently visited by the base policy, aligning collected trajectories with the generalist's deployment distribution while capturing recovery behaviors.

- In Stage 3 (fine-tuning), curated trajectories are distilled back into the generalist with standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT), applicable to both flow-matching and autoregressive heads.

**Results:**

PLD achieves a near-saturated 99% task success rate on the LIBERO benchmark.

## Overview

LIBERO-Plus is a comprehensive benchmark designed to establish a rigorous leaderboard for evaluating generalization capabilities across key vulnerability dimensions. The benchmark contains 10,030 tasks spanning seven perturbation dimensions.

## Seven Perturbation Dimensions

The perturbations are controlled across seven dimensions: object layouts, camera viewpoints, robot initial states, language instructions, lighting conditions, background textures, and sensor noise.

## Key Findings on VLA Robustness

The evaluation reveals significant vulnerabilities in current VLA models:

- **Camera and Robot State Sensitivity**: Models exhibit extreme sensitivity to perturbation factors, including camera viewpoints and robot initial states, with performance dropping from 95% to below 30% under modest perturbations.

- **Language Instruction Weakness**: Language perturbations result in the smallest average performance drop across most models, with models showing surprising insensitivity to language. Even without any valid language input, the performance of some models remained largely unchanged.

- **Positional Bias**: When target objects' placement is altered, model performance drops significantly, suggesting models may have learned positional information rather than task-relevant semantics, exhibiting positional bias rather than genuine semantic understanding.

## Benchmark Structure

The benchmark construction follows a systematic two-stage process: expanding the original LIBERO benchmark through seven distinct perturbation factors followed by task filtering and balancing, and evaluating the resulting tasks using four representative models stratifying them into five difficulty levels.

## Implicit Q-Learning (IQL) Overview

Implicit Q-Learning (IQL) uses in-sample value estimation and expectile regression to robustly learn policies solely from offline data in reinforcement learning. IQL approximates the policy improvement step implicitly by treating the state value function as a random variable, and taking a state conditional upper expectile of this random variable to estimate the value of the best actions in that state, leveraging the generalization capacity of the function approximator without ever directly querying a Q-function with unseen actions.

## Value and Advantage Decomposition

The IQL framework decomposes the learning into key components: IQL decouples value learning from policy learning with a state value function that learns via expectile regression, a critic Q-value function that fits action values with Bellman regression, and an actor policy model that updates the policy with advantage-weighted behavior cloning.

## Robot and Dense Reward Applications

Notable applications include robotic manipulation with symmetries, where SO(2)-equivariant IQL networks achieve higher sample efficiency in low-data regimes by leveraging geometric priors. Additionally, research investigates the performance of IQL in both dense and sparse reward settings within robotic environments like the ANT continous control environment.

## Offline RL Advantages

IQL methods and related implicit Q-learning frameworks are increasingly found in domains requiring stable offline policy improvement, robustness to distributional shift, or efficiency in high-risk, real-world settings. IQL demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on D4RL, a standard benchmark for offline reinforcement learning.

Posterior-Transition Reweighting (PTR) is a reward-free and conservative post-training method that decides how much each training sample should influence the supervised update.

For each sample, PTR encodes the observed post-action consequence as a latent target, inserts it into a candidate pool of mismatched targets, and uses a separate transition scorer to estimate a softmax identification posterior over target indices.

A lightweight consequence encoder and transition scorer produce per-sample weights from observed post-action consequences, without requiring reward labels or a tractable policy likelihood.

The method addresses a key challenge in robot learning: robot datasets are heterogeneous: they mix embodiments, camera setups, and demonstrations of varying quality, so many trajectories reflect recovery behavior, inconsistent operator skill, or weakly informative supervision. Rather than uniformly trusting all recorded supervision, PTR reallocates credit according to how attributable each sample's post-action consequence is under the current representation, improving conservative offline adaptation to heterogeneous robot data.

## RoboMimic Framework Overview

RoboMimic is a framework for robot learning from demonstration that offers a broad set of demonstration datasets collected on robot manipulation domains and learning algorithms to learn from these datasets.

## Demonstration Quality and Evaluation

The robomimic datasets supply large-scale human teleoperation demonstrations at varying qualities (expert/medium/mixed), enabling imitation and offline RL benchmarks with consistent metrics and baselines. The multi-human datasets from the RoboMimic benchmark include 100 demonstrations from each of three robot operators for three tasks in increasing difficulty: "Lift" where the robot simply lifts a cube, "Can" where the robot moves a can from one bin to another, and "Square" where the robot places a nut onto a peg. RoboMimic provides quality labels for each operator, which are used to assign quality scores (with scores of 1, 2, and 3 for the "worse", "okay", and "better" demonstrations respectively).

## Recent Research on Data Curation

Recent work has utilized RoboMimic's quality labels for demonstration curation evaluation. Researchers have assessed average quality of demonstrations remaining in datasets after filtering with different choices on the Lift, Can, and Square Multi-Human datasets from the Robomimic benchmark. This research explores methods for curating demonstration data using mutual information estimators and other curation techniques to improve downstream policy learning performance.

Based on my research, I have a clear picture now. Here are the critical findings:

1. **LIBERO is completely saturated**: PLD (99%) and SimpleVLA-RL (99.1%) leave essentially zero headroom
2. **LIBERO-Plus** (CVPR 2026) drops models from 95% to <30% under perturbations — huge headroom and much more discriminative
3. **Robometer already demonstrates reward-based data retrieval for IL** — the "reward-only" baseline is nearly already published
4. **SimpleVLA-RL achieves 91.7% from ONE trajectory + RL** — undermining the value of curating many demos for standard LIBERO

The fundamental issue: absolute performance on standard LIBERO is the wrong goal. The real value of smart curation is **robustness** (policies that handle perturbations) and **data efficiency** (same performance with less data). This calls for a **major revision** of the framing and evaluation, while keeping the core V/A decomposition insight.

The key new insight: reward-only curation biases toward "ideal condition" demonstrations (high reward = high progress = common trajectories), creating a coverage gap at test time under perturbations. V×A curation can explicitly preserve "high A at diverse V" — teaching adaptive behavior across varied states — producing more robust policies.

These bounds are not vacuous — we empirically validate the predicted coverage-robustness relationship on LIBERO-Plus. Tertiary benchmark: RoboMimic Multi-Human (3 tasks × 3 operator qualities — a natural mixed-quality setting where V/A decomposition should be especially valuable).
